contenido: 1. Called to salvation through faith in Jesus Christ, “true light that illuminates every man” ( [+[0]+] ), men become “light in the Lord” and “sons of light” ( [+[1]+] ), and are sanctified “by obeying the truth” ( [+[2]+] ).

2. No man can avoid the fundamental questions: what should I do? How can I discern good from evil? The answer is possible only thanks to the splendor of truth that shines in the most intimate part of the human spirit, as the psalmist says: «Many say: "Who will make us see happiness?" Lift up the light of your face upon us, Lord! ( [+[0]+] ).

3. The pastors of the Church, in communion with the Successor of Peter, are always close to the faithful in this effort, they accompany and guide them with their teaching, finding always new expressions of love and mercy to address not only believers but also all men of good will. The Second Vatican Council continues to be a privileged testimony of this attitude of the Church which, "expert in humanity" 5, places itself at the service of each man and the entire world 6.

4. Always, but especially in the last two centuries, the Supreme Pontiffs, either personally or together with the College of Bishops, have developed and proposed a moral teaching on the multiple and different areas of human life. In the name and with the authority of Jesus Christ, they have exhorted, denounced, explained; By fidelity to their mission, and committing themselves to the cause of man, they have confirmed, sustained, consoled; with the guarantee of the assistance of the Spirit of truth, they have contributed to a better understanding of the moral demands in the areas of human sexuality, the family, and social, economic and political life. His teaching, within the tradition of the Church and the history of humanity, represents a continuous deepening of moral knowledge 8.

5. In this "still current" context, I have made the decision to write, "as I already announced in the apostolic letter Spiritus Domini, published on August 1, 1987 on the occasion of the second centenary of the death of Saint Alphonsus Mary of Liguori," an encyclical intended to deal, "more broadly and deeply, with questions relating to the very foundations of moral theology." 9, fundamentals that are undermined by some current trends.

6. The dialogue of Jesus with the rich young man, recounted by Saint Matthew in chapter 19 of his gospel, can constitute a useful element to listen again in a living and penetrating way to his moral teaching: «One approached him and said to him: "Teacher, what good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?" He said to him, "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one Good. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments." "Which is it?" he tells her. And Jesus said, "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself." The young man says to him: "I have kept all this; what else am I missing?" Jesus said to him: "If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me" ( [+[0]+] ) 13.

7. "One approached him..." In the young man, whom Matthew's gospel does not name, we can recognize every man who, consciously or not, approaches Christ, redeemer of man, and asks him the moral question. For the young person, more than a question about the rules to be observed, it is a question of full meaning for life. Indeed, this is the central aspiration of every decision and every human action, the secret search and the intimate impulse that moves freedom. This question is, ultimately, an appeal to the absolute Good that attracts us and calls us to itself; It is the echo of God's call, origin and end of man's life. Precisely with this perspective, the Second Vatican Council has invited moral theology to be perfected, so that its exposition highlights the very high vocation that the faithful have received in Christ 14, the only answer that fully satisfies the longing of the human heart.

8. From the depth of the heart arises the question that the rich young man addresses to Jesus of Nazareth: an essential and unavoidable question for the life of every man, since it refers to the moral good that must be practiced and to eternal life. Jesus' interlocutor senses that there is a connection between moral good and the full fulfillment of one's own destiny. He is a pious Israelite who has grown up, we would say, in the shadow of the Law of the Lord. If he asks Jesus this question, we can imagine that he does not do so because he ignores the answer contained in the Law. It is more likely that his fascination with the person of Jesus caused new questions to arise in him about moral good. He feels the need to confront the one who had begun his preaching with this new and decisive announcement: «The time has come and the kingdom of God is near; convert and believe in the good news” ( [+[0]+] ).

9. Jesus says: “Why do you ask me about what is good? Only One is the Good. But if you want to enter into life, keep the commandments” ( [+[0]+] ). In the versions of the evangelists Mark and Luke the question is formulated like this: «Why do you call me good? No one is good but only God” ( [+[1]+] ).

10. The Church, enlightened by the words of the Master, believes that man, made in the image of the Creator, redeemed with the blood of Christ and sanctified by the presence of the Holy Spirit, has as the ultimate goal of his life to be "praise of the glory" of God ([+[0]+]), thus making each of his actions reflect his splendor. "Know yourself, beautiful soul: you are the image of God," writes Saint Ambrose. Know yourself, man: you are the glory of God ( [+[1]+] ). Hear how you are his glory. The prophet says: Your knowledge is mysterious to me ( [+[2]+] ), that is: your majesty is most admirable in my work, your wisdom is exalted in the mind of man. As I consider myself, whom you scrutinize in secret thoughts and intimate feelings, I recognize the mysteries of your science. Therefore, know yourself, man, how great you are and watch over yourself..." 17.

11. The statement that "only one is Good" thus refers us to the "first table" of the commandments, which requires recognizing God as the sole and absolute Lord, and worshiping him alone because he is infinitely holy ([+[0]+]). Goodness is belonging to God, obeying Him, walking humbly with Him practicing justice and loving piety ([+[1]+]). Recognizing the Lord as God is the fundamental core, the heart of the Law, from which the particular precepts are derived and to which they are ordered. Through the morality of the commandments, the belonging of the people of Israel to the Lord is manifested, because only God is the one who is "Good." This is the testimony of sacred Scripture, whose pages are penetrated by the living perception of the absolute holiness of God: "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts" ([+[2]+]).

12. Only God can answer the question about good because he is the Good. But God already answered this question: he did so by creating man and ordering him to his end with wisdom and love, through the law inscribed in his heart ( [+[0]+] ), the "natural law." This “is nothing more than the light of intelligence infused into us by God. Thanks to it we know what to do and what to avoid. God gave this light and this law in creation" 19. He then did so in the history of Israel, particularly with the "ten words", that is, with the commandments of Sinai, through which he founded the people of the Covenant ( [+[1]+] ) and called them to be his "personal property among all peoples", "a holy nation" ( [+[2]+] ), which would make its holiness shine among all nations ( [+[3]+] ). The delivery of the Decalogue is a promise and sign of the new covenant, when the law will be written again and definitively in the heart of man ([+[4]+]), to replace the law of sin, which had disfigured that heart ([+[5]+]). Then "a new heart" will be given because "a new spirit" will dwell in it, the Spirit of God ( [+[6]+] ) 20.

13. Jesus' answer is still not enough for the young man, who insists by asking the Master about the commandments that must be observed: «"Which ones?" he says to him» ([+[0]+]). He questions him about what he should do in life to bear witness to the holiness of God. After having directed the young man's attention to God, Jesus reminds him of the commandments of the Decalogue that refer to his neighbor: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, honor your father and mother, and love your neighbor as yourself." ( [+[1]+] ).

14. All this does not mean that Christ intends to give precedence to love of neighbor or separate it from love of God. This is confirmed by his dialogue with the doctor of the law, who asks a question very similar to that of the young man. Jesus refers him to the two commandments of love of God and love of neighbor ( [+[0]+] ) and invites him to remember that only their observance leads to eternal life: "Do that and you will live" ( [+[1]+] ). It is, therefore, significant that it is precisely the second of these commandments that arouses the curiosity and the question of the doctor of the law: "Who is my neighbor?" ( [+[2]+] ). The Master responds with the parable of the good Samaritan, the parable-key to the full understanding of the commandment to love one's neighbor ( [+[3]+] ).

15. In the "Sermon on the Mount", which constitutes the Magna Carta of evangelical morality 24, Jesus says: "Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law and the prophets. I have not come to abolish, but to fulfill” ( [+[0]+] ). Christ is the key to the Scriptures: "You search the Scriptures, they are the ones that testify about me" ( [+[1]+] ); He is the center of the economy of salvation, the recapitulation of the Old and New Testaments, of the promises of the Law and their fulfillment in the Gospel; he is the living and eternal link between the old and the new covenant. For his part, Saint Ambrose, commenting on Paul's text in which he says: "the end of the law is Christ" ([+[2]+]), affirms that it is "the end not as a defect, but as a fullness of the law; which is fulfilled in Christ ( [+[3]+] ), because he did not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it. Just as, although there is an Old Testament, all truth is contained in the New, so it is with the law: that which was given through Moses is a figure of the true law. Therefore, the mosaic is an image of the truth" 25.

16. The answer about the commandments does not satisfy the young man, who again asks Jesus: «I have kept all these; What else am I missing? ( [+[0]+] ). It is not easy to say with a clear conscience "I have kept all this", if one understands the full scope of the demands contained in the Law of God. However, although the rich young man is capable of giving such an answer; Although he has truly put the moral ideal into practice with seriousness and generosity since childhood, he knows that he is still far from the goal; In fact, before the person of Jesus he realizes that something is still missing. Jesus, in his last response, refers to this awareness that something is still missing: understanding the nostalgia for a fullness that surpasses the legalistic interpretation of the commandments, the good Teacher invites the young man to embark on the path of perfection: «If you want to be perfect, go, sell what you have and give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” ( [+[1]+] ).

17. We do not know to what extent the young man in the gospel understood the deep and demanding content of the first answer given by Jesus: "If you want to enter life, keep the commandments"; However, it is true that the affirmation expressed by the young man of having respected all the moral demands of the commandments constitutes the indispensable ground on which the desire for perfection can sprout and mature, that is, the realization of its meaning through the following of Christ. Jesus' conversation with the young man helps us understand the conditions for the moral growth of the man called to perfection: the young man, who has observed all the commandments, shows himself incapable of taking the next step with his strength alone. To do so requires mature freedom ( [+[0]+] ) and the divine gift of grace ( [+[1]+] ).

18. He who "lives according to the flesh" feels the law of God as a burden, indeed, as a denial or, in any way, as a restriction of his own freedom. On the other hand, those who are moved by love and "live according to the Spirit" ( [+[0]+] ), and wish to serve others, find in the law of God the fundamental and necessary path to practice love freely chosen and lived. Furthermore, he feels the inner urgency - a true and proper need, and no longer a constriction - to not stop at the minimum demands of the law, but to live them to the fullest. It is a path that is still uncertain and fragile while we are on earth, but one that grace makes possible by giving us the full "freedom of the children of God" ( [+[1]+] ) and, consequently, the ability to respond in moral life to the sublime vocation of being "children in the Son."

19. The path and, at the same time, the content of this perfection consists in the sequela Christi, in following Jesus, after having renounced one's own goods and oneself. Precisely this is the conclusion of Jesus' conversation with the young man: "then come and follow me" ([+[0]+]). It is an invitation whose wonderful depth will be fully understood by the disciples after Christ's resurrection, when the Holy Spirit will guide them into the full truth ( [+[1]+] ).

20. Jesus asks that they follow and imitate him in the path of love, a love that is given totally to brothers for the love of God: "This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you" ([+[0]+]). This “how” demands the imitation of Jesus, the imitation of his love, the sign of which is the washing of the feet: “If then I, the Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also must wash one another's feet. For I have given you an example, so that you also may do as I have done for you” ( [+[1]+] ). The way of acting of Jesus and his words, his actions and his precepts constitute the moral rule of the Christian life. Indeed, these actions of his and, in a particular way, the supreme act of his passion and death on the cross, are the living revelation of his love for the Father and for men. This is the love that Jesus asks all who follow him to imitate. It is the “new” commandment: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another. That, as I have loved you, so you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples: if you have love for one another” ( [+[2]+] ).

21. Following Christ is not an external imitation, because it affects man in his deepest interiority. To be a disciple of Jesus means to conform to him, who became a servant of all until the gift of himself on the cross ( [+[0]+] ). Through faith, Christ dwells in the heart of the believer ([+[1]+]), the disciple resembles his Lord and is configured to him; which is the fruit of grace, of the operating presence of the Holy Spirit in us.

22. The conclusion of Jesus' conversation with the rich young man is bitter: "When the young man heard these words, he went away saddened, because he had many possessions" ([+[0]+]). Not only the rich man, but also the disciples themselves are frightened by Jesus' call to follow him, whose demands exceed human aspirations and forces: "When the disciples heard this, filled with astonishment, they said: 'Then who can be saved?'" ([+[1]+]). But the Master puts the power of God before our eyes: "With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible" ([+[2]+]).

23. "The law of the Spirit who gives life in Christ Jesus freed you from the law of sin and death" ( [+[0]+] ). With these words the apostle Paul introduces us to consider in the perspective of the history of salvation that is fulfilled in Christ the relationship between the law ([+[1]+]) and grace ([+[2]+]). He recognizes the pedagogical function of the law, which, by allowing sinful man to value his own helplessness and removing the presumption of self-sufficiency, opens him to the invocation and acceptance of "life in the Spirit." Only in this new life is it possible to practice God's commandments. Indeed, it is by faith in Christ that we are justified ( [+[3]+] ): the justice that the law demands, but that it cannot give, is found by every believer manifested and granted by the Lord Jesus. In this way Saint Augustine admirably summarizes the Pauline dialectic between law and grace: «For this reason, the law was given so that grace might be implored; grace has been given so that the law might be observed" 30.

24. In this way, the true and original face of the commandment of love and the perfection to which it is ordered is manifested; It is a possibility open to man exclusively by grace, by the gift of God, by his love. On the other hand, precisely the awareness of having received the gift, of possessing the love of God in Jesus Christ, generates and sustains the responsible response of a full love towards God and among one's brothers, as the apostle Saint John insistently reminds us in his first letter: "Dear friends, let us love one another, since love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. He who does not love has not known God, because God is Love... Dear ones, if God loved us in this way, we too must love one another... Let us love, because he loved us first" ( [+[0]+] ).

25. Jesus' conversation with the rich young ruler continues, in a certain sense, in every era of history; also today. The question: "Teacher, what good must I do to obtain eternal life?" It springs up in the heart of every man, and it is always and only Christ who offers the full and definitive answer. The Master who teaches the commandments of God, who invites us to follow and gives grace for a new life, is always present and active among us, according to his promise: "Behold, I am with you every day until the end of the world" ([+[0]+]). The contemporaneity of Christ with respect to the man of each era is realized in the living body of the Church. For this reason the Lord promised his disciples the Holy Spirit, who would "remember" them and make them understand his commandments ([+[1]+]), and, at the same time, would be the fundamental principle of a new life for the world ([+[2]+]).

26. In the moral catechesis of the Apostles, along with exhortations and indications related to the historical and cultural context, there is an ethical teaching with precise norms of behavior. This is what emerges in his letters, which contain the interpretation "under the guidance of the Holy Spirit" of the Lord's precepts that must be lived in diverse cultural circumstances ( [+[0]+] ). Charged with preaching the Gospel, the Apostles, by virtue of their pastoral responsibility, monitored, from the origins of the Church, the right conduct of Christians 35, while at the same time they monitored the purity of the faith and the transmission of divine gifts through the sacraments 36. The first Christians, coming from both the Jewish people and the Gentiles, were differentiated from the pagans not only by their faith and their liturgy, but also by the testimony of their conduct. moral, inspired by the new Law37. Indeed, the Church is both a communion of faith and life; Its standard is “faith acting through charity” ( [+[1]+] ).

27. Promoting and safeguarding, in the unity of the Church, faith and moral life is the mission entrusted by Jesus to the Apostles ([+[0]+]), which is continued in the ministry of his successors. It is what is found in the living Tradition, through which – as the Second Vatican Council states – “the Church with its teaching, its life, its worship, preserves and transmits to all ages what it is and what it believes. This Apostolic Tradition grows in the Church with the help of the Holy Spirit." 39. In the Spirit, the Church welcomes and transmits the Scripture as a testimony of the wonders that God has done in history ([+[1]+]), confesses the truth of the Word made flesh with the lips of the Fathers and doctors, practices its precepts and charity in the lives of the saints, and in the sacrifice of the martyrs, celebrates its hope in the liturgy. Through Tradition, Christians receive "the living voice of the Gospel" 40, as a faithful expression of wisdom and divine will.

28. Meditation on the dialogue between Jesus and the rich young ruler has allowed us to gather the essential contents of the revelation of the Old and New Testaments on moral behavior. They are: the subordination of man and his actions to God, the only one who is "Good"; the relationship, clearly indicated in the divine commandments, between the moral good of human acts and eternal life; the following of Christ, which opens to man the perspective of perfect love; and finally, the gift of the Holy Spirit, source and force of the moral life of the "new creature" ( [+[0]+] ).

29. The moral reflection of the Church, always done in the light of Christ, the "good Teacher", has also developed in the specific form of theological science called moral theology; science that welcomes and challenges divine Revelation and responds at the same time to the demands of human reason. Moral theology is a reflection that concerns "morality", that is, the good and evil of human acts and the person who performs them, and in this sense it is open to all men; but it is also theology, insofar as it recognizes the beginning and the end of moral behavior in the only one who is Good and who, giving himself to man in Christ, offers him the beatitudes of divine life.

30. In addressing you with this encyclical, brothers in the episcopate, I wish to enunciate the principles necessary for the discernment of what is contrary to "sound doctrine", recalling those elements of the moral teaching of the Church that today seem particularly exposed to error, ambiguity or oblivion. On the other hand, they are elements on which depends the "answer to the hidden enigmas of the human condition that, today as yesterday, intimately move hearts: What is man? What is the meaning and purpose of our life? What is good and what is sin? What is the origin and end of pain? What is the path to achieving true happiness? What is death, judgment and retribution after death? What "Is it, finally, that ultimate and ineffable mystery that encompasses our existence, from which we come and towards which we are heading?" 50.
31. The human problems most debated and resolved in a diverse way in contemporary moral reflection are related, although in a different way, to a crucial problem: the freedom of man.

32. In some currents of modern thought, freedom has been exalted to the point of considering it as an absolute, which would be the source of values. Doctrines that ignore the meaning of the transcendent or those that are explicitly atheistic are oriented in this direction. The prerogatives of a supreme instance of moral judgment, which categorically and infallibly decides on good and evil, have been attributed to the individual conscience. To the assumption that one must follow one's own conscience has been improperly added the affirmation that moral judgment is true by the very fact that it comes from conscience. But, in this way, the necessary demand for truth has disappeared in favor of a criterion of sincerity, of authenticity, of "agreement with oneself", in such a way that a radically subjectivist conception of moral judgment has been reached.

33. Parallel to the exaltation of freedom, and paradoxically in contrast to it, modern culture radically questions this same freedom. A set of disciplines, grouped under the name "human sciences", have precisely called attention to the psychological and social conditions that weigh on the exercise of human freedom. The knowledge of such conditions and the attention paid to them are important advances that have found application in various areas of existence, such as in pedagogy or in the administration of justice. But some of them, going beyond the conclusions that can legitimately be drawn from these observations, have come to question or even deny the very reality of human freedom.

34. "Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?" The moral question, to which Christ answers, cannot ignore the problem of freedom, in fact, he considers it central, because there is no morality without freedom: "Man can be converted to good only in freedom" 56. But what freedom? The Council - in the face of those contemporaries of ours who "so defend" freedom and who "ardently seek it", but who "often cultivate it in a bad way, as if everything were lawful as long as it is liked, even evil" - presents true freedom: "True freedom is an eminent sign of the divine image in man. For God wanted to "leave man in the hands of his own decision" ([+[0]+]), so that he may seek without coercion his Creator and, by adhering to him, freely reach full and happy perfection." 57. If there is the right to be respected in one's own path of search for truth, there is even before that the moral obligation, grave for each one, to seek the truth and to follow it once known 58. In this sense, Cardinal J. H. Newman, A great defender of the rights of conscience, he stated decisively: "Conscience has rights because it has duties" 59.

35. We read in the book of Genesis: «God imposed this commandment on man: "You can eat from any tree in the garden, but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you will not eat, because in the day that you eat from it, you will die without remedy"» ([+[0]+]).

36. The demand for autonomy that exists today has not ceased to exert its influence even in the field of Catholic moral theology. Indeed, although it has never attempted to oppose human freedom to divine law, nor to question the existence of an ultimate religious foundation for moral norms, it has nevertheless been led to a profound rethinking of the role of reason and faith in the establishment of moral norms that refer to specific "intramundane" behaviors, that is, with respect to oneself, others and the world of things.

37. Wanting, however, to maintain moral life in a Christian context, some moralist theologians have introduced a clear distinction, contrary to Catholic doctrine 63, between an ethical order “which would have human origin and only worldly value,” and an order of salvation, for which only some interior intentions and attitudes before God and neighbor would be important. Consequently, we have reached the point of denying the existence, in divine Revelation, of a specific and determined moral content, universally valid and permanent: the Word of God would be limited to proposing an exhortation, a generic parentesis, which then only autonomous reason would have the task of filling with truly "objective" normative determinations, that is, appropriate to the specific historical situation. Naturally, an autonomy conceived in this way also entails the denial of a specific doctrinal competence on the part of the Church and its teaching regarding certain moral norms related to the so-called "human good." These would not belong to the proper content of the Revelation and would not be important in themselves in order to salvation.

38. Citing the words of the Ecclesiasticus, the Second Vatican Council thus explains the "true freedom" that in man is "an eminent sign of the divine image": "God wanted to "leave man in the hands of his own will", so that he would seek without constraint his Creator and, adhering to him, freely reach full and happy perfection." 64. These words indicate the wonderful depth of participation in divine sovereignty, to which man has been called; They indicate that the sovereignty of man extends, in a certain way, over man himself. This is an aspect constantly highlighted in theological reflection on human freedom, interpreted in terms of a form of kingship. For example, Saint Gregory Niseno says: «The spirit manifests its royalty and excellence... in its being without an owner and free, governing itself autocratically with its will. Who else is this proper to but the king?... Thus human nature, created to be master of other creatures, by its resemblance to the sovereign of the universe was constituted as a living image, a participant in the dignity and name of the Archetype" 65.

39. Not only the world, but also man himself has been entrusted to his own care and responsibility. God has left him “in the hands of his own will” ( [+[0]+] ), so that he may seek his creator and freely achieve perfection. Achieving means personally building this perfection in oneself. In fact, just as by governing the world man shapes it according to his intelligence and will, so by performing morally good acts, man confirms, develops and consolidates in himself the resemblance to God.

40. The teaching of the Council emphasizes, on the one hand, the activity of human reason when it determines the application of the moral law: the moral life requires the creativity and ingenuity proper to the person, the origin and cause of his deliberate acts. On the other hand, reason finds its truth and authority in the eternal law, which is nothing other than divine wisdom itself 69. Moral life is based, therefore, on the principle of a "just autonomy" 70 of man, the personal subject of his actions. The moral law comes from God and always has its origin in him. By virtue of natural reason, which derives from divine wisdom, the moral law is, at the same time, man's own law. In fact, natural law, as has been seen, “is nothing other than the light of intelligence infused into us by God. Thanks to it we know what to do and what to avoid. "God has given this light and this law in creation" 71. The just autonomy of practical reason means that man possesses within himself his own law, received from the Creator. However, the autonomy of reason cannot mean the creation, by reason itself, of moral values and norms 72. If this autonomy implied a denial of the participation of practical reason in the wisdom of the divine Creator and Legislator, or if a creative freedom of moral norms were suggested, according to historical contingencies or the various societies and cultures, such alleged autonomy would contradict the teaching of the Church on the truth of man 73. It would be the death of true freedom: "But you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, for in the day that you eat of it, you shall surely die" ([+[0]+]).

41. The true moral autonomy of man does not at all mean the rejection, but rather the acceptance of the moral law, of God's command: "God imposed this commandment on man..." ( [+[0]+] ). The freedom of man and the law of God meet and are called to interpenetrate each other, in the sense of man's free obedience to God and God's free benevolence to man. And, therefore, obedience to God is not, as some think, a heteronomy, as if moral life were subject to the will of an absolute omnipotence, external to man and contrary to the affirmation of his freedom. In reality, if heteronomy of morality meant denial of man's self-determination or imposition of norms foreign to his good, such heteronomy would be in contradiction with the revelation of the Covenant and the redeeming Incarnation, and would be nothing more than a form of alienation, contrary to divine wisdom and the dignity of the human person.

42. The freedom of man, modeled after that of God, is not only not denied by his obedience to the divine law, but only through this obedience does it remain in the truth and is in accordance with the dignity of man, as the Council clearly says: "The dignity of man requires, in fact, that he act according to a conscious and free choice, that is, moved and induced personally from within and not under the pressure of a blind internal impulse or mere external coercion. Man achieves this dignity when, freeing himself from all slavery to the passions, he pursues his goal in the free choice of good and effectively and skilfully procures the appropriate means for this" 75. Man, in his tendency towards God - "the only Good" - must freely do good and avoid evil. But for this man must be able to distinguish good from evil. And this happens, above all, thanks to the light of natural reason, a reflection in man of the splendor of the face of God. In this regard, commenting on a verse from Psalm 4, Saint Thomas states: «The psalmist, after having said: "sacrifice a sacrifice of righteousness" ([+[0]+]), adds, to those who ask what are the works of justice: "Many say: Who will show us good?"; and, in answer to this question, he says: "The light of your face, Lord, has been impressed on our minds," as if the light of natural reason, by which we discern good and evil - such is the purpose of the natural law - were nothing other than the divine light impressed on us. that it is promulgated is typical of human nature77.

43. The Second Vatican Council recalls that “the supreme norm of human life is the same divine, eternal, objective and universal law by which God orders, directs and governs, with the design of his wisdom and his love, the world and the paths of the human community. God makes man a participant in this law of his, so that man, as divine Providence has gently ordained, can increasingly recognize the immutable truth" 78.

44. The Church has often referred to the Thomistic doctrine on natural law, assuming it in its moral teaching. Thus, my venerated predecessor Leo XIII highlighted the essential subordination of reason and human law to the wisdom of God and his law. After stating that "the natural law is written and engraved in the minds of all men and of each man, since it is nothing other than the same human reason that commands us to do good and tells us not to sin," Leo XIII refers to the "highest reason" of the divine Legislator. "But such a prescription of human reason could not have the force of law if it were not the voice and interpreter of a higher reason, to which our spirit and our freedom must be subject." Indeed, the force of the law lies in its authority to impose duties, grant rights and sanction certain behaviors: "Now, all this could not occur in man if he himself, as supreme legislator, gave himself the norm for his actions." And he concludes: «From this it follows that the natural law is the same eternal law, inherent in beings endowed with reason, which inclines them to the act and the end that suits them; It is the same eternal reason of the Creator and governor of the universe" 83.

45. The Church welcomes with recognition and guards with love the entire deposit of Revelation, treating it with religious respect and fulfilling its mission of interpreting the law of God authentically in the light of the Gospel. Furthermore, the Church receives as a gift the new Law, which is the "fulfillment" of the law of God in Jesus Christ and in his Spirit. It is an “internal” law ( [+[0]+] ), “written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tables of stone, but on tables of flesh, in the hearts” ( [+[1]+] ); a law of perfection and freedom ( [+[2]+] ); It is “the law of the spirit that gives life in Christ Jesus” ( [+[3]+] ). About this law Saint Thomas says: «This can be called law in a double sense. Firstly, the law of the spirit is the Holy Spirit... who, by indwelling the soul, not only teaches what needs to be done by illuminating the understanding about the things that need to be done, but also inclines one to act rightly... Secondly, the law of the spirit can be called the proper effect of the Holy Spirit, that is, the faith that acts through charity ([+[4]+] ), which, for this very reason, teaches internally about the things that need to be done... and inclines the affection to act" 84.

46. ​​The alleged conflict between freedom and law is reconsidered today with singular force in relation to natural law and, in particular, in relation to nature. In reality, debates about nature and freedom have always accompanied the history of moral reflection, assuming heated tones with the Renaissance and the Reformation, as can be seen in the teachings of the Council of Trent 85. The contemporary era is marked, although in a different sense, by an analogous tension. The taste for empirical observation, the procedures of scientific objectification, technical progress, and some forms of liberalism have led to contrasting the two terms, as if the dialectic – and even the conflict – between freedom and nature were a structural characteristic of human history. In other times it seemed that "nature" completely subjected man to its dynamisms and even its determinisms. Even today the spatio-temporal coordinates of the sensible world, the physical-chemical constants, corporeal dynamisms, psychic drives and social conditioning seem to many to be the only truly decisive factors of human realities. In this context, even moral facts, regardless of their specificity, are often considered as if they were statistically verifiable data, as behaviors observable or explainable only with the categories of psycho-social mechanisms. And so some ethics scholars, who by profession examine the actions and actions of man, may feel the temptation to value their knowledge, and even their standards of action, according to a statistical result on concrete human behaviors and the moral opinions of the majority.

47. In this context, the objections of physicalism and naturalism have arisen against the traditional conception of natural law. This would present as moral laws those that in themselves would only be biological laws. Thus, very superficially, a permanent and immutable character would be attributed to some human behaviors, and, on that basis, universally valid moral norms would be sought to be formulated. According to some theologians, such a biological or naturalistic argument would even be present in some documents of the Magisterium of the Church, especially those related to the field of sexual and marital ethics. Based on a naturalistic conception of the sexual act, contraception, direct sterilization, autoeroticism, premarital relations, homosexual relations, as well as artificial fertilization would be condemned as morally inadmissible. Now, according to the opinion of these theologians, the morally negative assessment of such acts would not adequately consider the rational and free character of man, nor the cultural conditioning of each moral norm. They say that man, as a rational being, not only can, but must even freely decide the meaning of his behaviors. This decision on meaning should obviously take into account the multiple limits of the human being, who has a corporeal and historical condition. Additionally, you should consider behavioral models and the meaning they have in a given culture. And, above all, it should respect the fundamental commandment of love for God and neighbor. They also affirm that, however, God has created man as a rationally free being; He has left him "in the hands of his own will" and expects from him his own, rational formation of his life. Love for one's neighbor would mean above all or exclusively a respect for his free decision about himself. The mechanisms of man's own behavior, as well as the so-called natural inclinations, would establish to the maximum - as they say - a general orientation of correct behavior, but they could not determine the moral evaluation of each human act, so complex from the point of view of the situations.

48. Given this interpretation, it is worth looking carefully at the correct relationship between freedom and human nature, and, specifically, the place that the human body has in questions of natural law.

49. A doctrine that separates the moral act from the corporeal dimensions of its exercise is contrary to the teachings of sacred Scripture and Tradition. Such doctrine revives, in new forms, some old errors always combated by the Church, because they reduce the human person to a spiritual, purely formal freedom. This reduction ignores the moral meaning of the body and its behaviors ( [+[0]+] ). The apostle Paul declares those “impure, idolaters, adulterers, effeminate, homosexuals, thieves, covetous, drunkards, revilers and raptors” excluded from the kingdom of heaven ([+[1]+]). This condemnation – cited by the 88th Council of Trent – ​​lists as mortal sins, or infamous practices, some specific behaviors whose voluntary acceptance prevents believers from having a share in the promised inheritance. In fact, body and soul are inseparable: in the person, in the voluntary agent and in the deliberate act, they are or are lost together.

50. This is how the true meaning of natural law can be understood, which refers to the proper and original nature of man, to the "nature of the human person" 89, which is the person himself in the unity of soul and body; in the unity of its spiritual and biological inclinations, as well as all other specific characteristics, necessary to achieve its goal. «The natural moral law evidences and prescribes the purposes, rights and duties, based on the corporal and spiritual nature of the human person. This law cannot be understood as a simply biological normativity, but must be conceived as the rational order by which man is called by the Creator to direct and regulate his life and actions and, more specifically, to use and dispose of his own body. In this way, human life, being a fundamental good of man, acquires a moral meaning in relation to the good of the person that must always be affirmed by himself: while it is always morally illicit to kill an innocent human being, it can be lawful, laudable and even obligatory to give one's life ( [+[0]+] ) for love of one's neighbor or to bear witness to the truth. In fact, only with reference to the human person in his "unified totality", that is, "soul expressing itself in the body informed by an immortal spirit" 91, can the specifically human meaning of the body be understood. In fact, natural inclinations have a moral importance only when they refer to the human person and its authentic realization, which is always and only verified in human nature. The Church, by rejecting the manipulations of corporeality that alter its human meaning, serves man and shows him the path of true love, the only means to find the true God.

51. The alleged conflict between freedom and nature also has repercussions on the interpretation of some specific aspects of natural law, mainly on its universality and immutability. «Where, then, are these rules written, Saint Augustine asks...but in the book of that light called truth? From here, then, all just law derives and acts rightly in the heart of the man who works justice, not coming out of him, but as if imprinting itself on him, as the image passes from the ring to the wax, but without leaving the ring" 92.

52. It is just and good, always and for everyone, to serve God, give him due worship and honor parents properly. These positive precepts, which prescribe carrying out some actions and cultivating certain attitudes, are universally binding; are immutable 94; They unite in the same common good all men of each era of history, created for "the same divine vocation and destiny" 95. These universal and permanent laws correspond to knowledge of practical reason and are applied to particular acts through the judgment of conscience. The acting subject personally assimilates the truth contained in the law; He appropriates and makes this truth of his being his own through his actions and the corresponding virtues. The negative precepts of natural law are universally valid: they bind everyone, always and in all circumstances. In effect, these are prohibitions that prohibit a certain action "semper et pro semper", without exceptions, because the choice of that behavior is in no case compatible with the goodness of the will of the person who acts, with his vocation to life with God and communion with his neighbor. It is forbidden for each person and always to violate precepts that bind everyone and no matter what the cost, and to harm others and, above all, themselves, the personal and common dignity of all.

53. The great sensitivity that contemporary man shows for historicity and culture leads some to doubt the immutability of natural law itself, and therefore the existence of "objective norms of morality" 96 valid for all men of yesterday, today and tomorrow. Is it possible to affirm as universally valid for everyone and always permanent certain rational determinations established in the past, when the progress that humanity would have made successively was unknown?

54. The relationship between man's freedom and the law of God has its basis in the heart of the person, that is, in his moral conscience: "Deep within his conscience," states the Second Vatican Council, "man discovers a law that he does not give to himself, but which he must obey and whose voice resonates, when necessary, in the ears of his heart, always calling him to love and do good and to avoid evil: do this, avoid that. Because man has a law written by God in his heart, in whose obedience lies human dignity and according to which he will be judged ( [+[0]+] )" 101.

55. According to the opinion of some theologians, the function of conscience would have been reduced, at least in a certain past, to a simple application of general moral norms to each case of the person's life. But such norms, they claim, are not capable of accepting and respecting all the unrepeatable specificity of all the concrete acts of people; In some way, they can help a fair assessment of the situation, but they cannot replace people in making a personal decision about how to behave in certain particular cases. Furthermore, the aforementioned criticism of the traditional interpretation of human nature and its importance for moral life leads some authors to affirm that these norms are not so much an objective binding criterion for judgments of conscience, but rather a general perspective that, at first, helps man to give an orderly approach to his personal and social life. Furthermore, they reveal the typical complexity of the phenomenon of consciousness: it is deeply related to the entire psychological and affective sphere, as well as to the multiple influences of the person's social and cultural environment. On the other hand, the value of conscience is exalted to the maximum, which the Council itself has defined "the tabernacle of man, in which he is alone with God, whose voice resonates in his most intimate part" 102. This voice, it is said, induces man not so much to a meticulous observance of universal norms, but rather to a creative and responsible acceptance of the personal tasks that God entrusts to him.

56. To justify such positions, some have proposed a kind of double status of moral truth. In addition to the doctrinal and abstract level, it would be necessary to recognize the originality of a certain more concrete existential consideration. This, taking into account the circumstances and the situation, could legitimately establish some exceptions to the general rule and thus allow the practical realization, with good conscience, of what is qualified by the moral law as intrinsically evil. In this way, in some cases a separation, or even an opposition, is established between the doctrine of the generally valid precept and the norm of individual conscience, which would in fact decide, ultimately, on good and evil. With this basis, the aim is to establish the legitimacy of the so-called pastoral solutions contrary to the teachings of the Magisterium, and to justify a creative hermeneutics, according to which moral conscience would not be obligated at all, in all cases, by a particular negative precept.

57. The same text of the letter to the Romans, which has presented to us the essence of the natural law, also indicates the biblical meaning of conscience, especially in its specific connection with the law: «When the Gentiles, who have no law, naturally fulfill the prescriptions of the law, without having a law, they are law to themselves; as those who show that they have the reality of that law written in their hearts, witnessed by their conscience with their conflicting judgments that accuse them and also defend them" ([+[0]+]).

58. The importance of this intimate dialogue between man and himself will never be adequately valued. But, in reality, this is man's dialogue with God, author of the law, first model and ultimate goal of man. «The conscience – says Saint Bonaventure – is like a herald of God and his messenger, and what it says it does not send by itself, but it sends it as coming from God, just like a herald when he proclaims the king's edict. And from this derives the fact that conscience has the power to oblige" 103. It can be said, then, that conscience bears witness to the righteousness or evil of man to man himself, but at the same time and even before, it is a witness to God himself, whose voice and whose judgment penetrate the intimacy of man to the roots of his soul, inviting him "fortiter et suaviter" to obedience: "Moral conscience does not lock man in an impassable solitude and impenetrable, but opens it to the call, to the voice of God. In this, and in nothing else, lies all the mystery and dignity of moral conscience: in being the place, the holy space where God speaks to man" 104.

59. Saint Paul does not limit himself to recognizing that conscience acts as a witness, but also manifests the way in which it performs such a function. These are arguments that accuse or defend pagans in relation to their behaviors ([+[0]+]). The term reasoning demonstrates the character of conscience, which is to be a moral judgment about man and his actions. It is a judgment of acquittal or condemnation depending on whether human acts are in accordance or not with the law of God written on the heart. Precisely, of the judgment of the acts and, at the same time, of their author and the moment of their definitive fulfillment, the apostle Paul speaks in the same text: this is how it will be "on the day when God will judge the secret actions of men, according to my gospel, by Christ Jesus" ([+[1]+]).

60. Like natural law itself and all practical knowledge, the judgment of conscience also has an imperative character: man must act in accordance with said judgment. If man acts against this judgment, or performs it even when he is not sure whether a certain act is correct or good, he is condemned by his own conscience, the next norm of personal morality. The dignity of this rational body and the authority of its voice and its judgments derive from the truth about moral good and evil, which it is called to listen to and express. This truth is indicated by the "divine law", a universal and objective standard of morality. The judgment of conscience does not establish the law, but rather affirms the authority of natural law and practical reason in relation to the supreme good, whose appeal the human person accepts and whose commandments he accepts: «Conscience, therefore, is not an autonomous and exclusive source for deciding what is good or bad; On the contrary, a principle of obedience to the objective norm is deeply engraved in it, which grounds and conditions the congruence of its decisions with the precepts and prohibitions on which human behavior is based" 106.

61. The truth about moral good, manifested in the law of reason, is recognized practically and concretely by the judgment of conscience, which leads to assuming responsibility for the good done and the evil committed; If man commits evil, the just judgment of his conscience is a witness to the universal truth of good, as well as the malice of his particular decision. But the verdict of conscience remains in man even as a sign of hope and mercy. While demonstrating the evil committed, he also remembers the forgiveness that must be asked, the good that must be practiced and the virtues that must always be cultivated, with the grace of God.

62. Conscience, as a judgment of an act, is not exempt from the possibility of error. «However, – says the Council – it often happens that conscience errs due to invincible ignorance, without losing its dignity. But this cannot be said when man does not concern himself with seeking the truth and the good and, little by little, due to the habit of sin, the conscience becomes almost blind." 107. With these brief words, the Council offers a synthesis of the doctrine that the Church has developed over the centuries on the erroneous conscience.

63. In any case, the dignity of conscience always derives from the truth: in the case of right conscience, it is the objective truth accepted by man; in that of erroneous conscience, it is about what man, making a mistake, subjectively considers true. It is never acceptable to confuse a subjective error about the moral good with the objective truth, rationally proposed to man by virtue of his end, nor to equate the moral value of the act carried out with a true and upright conscience, with that carried out following the judgment of an erroneous conscience 108. The evil committed due to invincible ignorance, or a non-culpable error of judgment, may not be attributable to the person who does it; But even in this case it is still an evil, a disorder in relation to the truth about the good. Furthermore, the unrecognized good does not contribute to the moral growth of the person who realizes it; This does not perfect it and does not serve to dispose it to the supreme good. Thus, before we feel easily justified in the name of our conscience, we must meditate on the words of the psalm: "Who realizes his errors? Cleanse me from hidden faults" ([+[0]+]). There are faults that we cannot see and that are nevertheless faults, because we have refused to walk towards the light ( [+[1]+] ).

64. In the words of Jesus mentioned above, we also find the call to form conscience, to make it the object of continuous conversion to truth and good. The Apostle's exhortation not to conform to the mentality of this world, but to "be transformed by renewing our minds" ([+[0]+]) is analogous. In reality, the heart converted to the Lord and to the love of goodness is the source of the true judgments of conscience. Indeed, in order to be able to "distinguish what the will of God is: what is good, what is pleasing, what is perfect" ([+[1]+]), knowledge of the law of God in general is necessary, but this is not enough: a kind of "connaturality" between man and the true good is indispensable 110. Such connaturality is based and develops in the virtuous attitudes of man himself: prudence and the other cardinal virtues, and first of all the theological virtues of faith, hope and charity. In this sense, Jesus said: "He who works the truth goes to the light" ( [+[2]+] ).

65. The interest in freedom, particularly acute today, leads many scholars of human or theological sciences to develop a more penetrating analysis of its nature and its dynamisms. It is precisely highlighted that freedom is not only the choice for this or that particular action; but it is also, within that choice, a decision about oneself and disposition of one's own life in favor or against the Good, in favor of or against the Truth; ultimately, for or against God. The eminent importance of some decisions that shape the entire moral life of a given man is precisely highlighted, configuring themselves as the channel in which other particular daily decisions may also be situated and developed.

66. There is no doubt that Christian moral doctrine, in its very biblical roots, recognizes the specific importance of a fundamental choice that qualifies the moral life and that compromises freedom at a radical level before God. It is about the choice of faith, the obedience of faith ([+[0]+]), by which "man gives himself entirely and freely to God, and offers him "the total homage of his understanding and will"" 112. This faith, which acts through charity ([+[1]+]), comes from the most intimate part of man, from his "heart" ([+[2]+]), and from here it is called to bear fruit in works ( [+[3]+] ). In the Decalogue we find, at the beginning of the various commandments, the fundamental clause: "I, the Lord, am your God" ([+[4]+]), which, conferring the original meaning to the multiple and various particular prescriptions, ensures to the morality of the Alliance a physiognomy of totality, unity and depth. Israel's fundamental choice therefore refers to the fundamental commandment ( [+[5]+] ). The morality of the new alliance is also dominated by the fundamental call of Jesus to follow him – he says to the young man: «If you want to be perfect... come, follow me» ( [+[6]+] )â; and the disciple responds to that call with a radical decision and choice. The evangelical parables of the treasure and the precious pearl, for which everything one possesses is sold, are eloquent and effective images of the radical and unconditional character of the election that the kingdom of God demands. The radical nature of the choice to follow Jesus is wonderfully expressed in his words: “Whoever wants to save his life will lose it; but whoever loses his life for me and for the Gospel will save it” ( [+[7]+] ).

67. Therefore, these theories are contrary to the same biblical teaching, which conceives the fundamental option as a true and proper choice of freedom and deeply links this choice to particular acts. Through fundamental choice, man is capable of directing his life and “with the help of grace” reaching its end following the divine call. But this capacity is in fact exercised in the particular choices of determined acts, through which man deliberately conforms to the will, wisdom and law of God. Therefore, it is stated that the so-called fundamental option, to the extent that it differs from a generic intention and, therefore, not yet determined in a binding form of freedom, is always acted upon through conscious and free choices. Precisely for this reason, the fundamental option is revoked when man compromises his freedom in conscious choices of the opposite direction, in serious moral matters.

68. However, it is necessary to add an important pastoral consideration. In the logic of the theories mentioned above, man, by virtue of a fundamental choice, could remain faithful to God regardless of the greater or lesser conformity of some of his choices and his concrete actions with specific moral norms or rules. By virtue of a primordial option for charity, man – according to these currents – could remain morally good, persevere in the grace of God, achieve his own salvation, even if some of his specific behaviors are deliberately and seriously contrary to the commandments of God.

69. The considerations surrounding the fundamental option, as we have seen, have induced some theologians to also subject the traditional distinction between mortal sins and venial sins to a profound revision; They emphasize that opposition to the law of God, which causes the loss of sanctifying grace – and, in the case of death in such a state of sin, eternal damnation – can only be the fruit of an act that commits the person as a whole, that is, an act of fundamental option. According to these theologians, mortal sin, which separates man from God, would be verified only in the rejection of God, which is carried out at a level of freedom not identifiable with an act of choice nor which can be reached with only reflexive knowledge. In this sense, they add, it is difficult, at least psychologically, to accept the fact that a Christian, who wants to remain united to Jesus Christ and his Church, can commit mortal sins so easily and repeatedly, as the very material of his actions sometimes seems to indicate. Likewise, it would be difficult to accept that man is capable, in a short period of time, of radically breaking the bond of communion with God and of successively converting to him through sincere penance. Therefore, it is necessary – it is stated – to measure the seriousness of sin according to the degree of commitment to freedom of the person who performs an act, and not according to the subject matter of said act.

70. The post-synodal apostolic exhortation Reconciliatio et paenitentia has confirmed the importance and permanent relevance of the distinction between mortal and venial sins, according to the tradition of the Church. And the Synod of Bishops of 1983, from which said exhortation emanated, "not only reaffirmed what was proclaimed by the Council of Trent regarding the existence and nature of mortal and venial sins, but also wanted to remember that a mortal sin is what has as its object a serious matter and that, furthermore, it is committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent" 116.

71. The relationship between the freedom of man and the law of God, which finds its vital and profound scope in moral conscience, is manifested and realized in human acts. It is precisely through his actions that man is perfected as such, as a person called to spontaneously seek his Creator and to freely achieve, through his adherence to him, happy and full perfection 119.

72. The morality of acts is defined by the relationship of man's freedom with authentic good. This good is established, as an eternal law, by the wisdom of God who orders every being to its end. This eternal law is known both through man's natural reason ([+[0]+]), and “in an integral and perfect way” through the supernatural revelation of God ([+[1]+]). Acting is morally good when the choices of freedom are in accordance with the true good of man and thus express the voluntary ordering of the person towards his ultimate end, that is, God himself: the supreme good in which man finds his full and perfect happiness. The initial question of the young man's dialogue with Jesus: "What good must I do to obtain eternal life?" ( [+[2]+] ) immediately demonstrates the essential link between the moral value of an act and the ultimate goal of man. Jesus, in his response, confirms the conviction of his interlocutor: the fulfillment of good acts, commanded by the only one who is "Good", constitutes the indispensable condition and the path to eternal happiness: "If you want to enter into life, keep the commandments" ([+[3]+]). Jesus' response referring to the commandments also shows that the path to the end is marked by respect for the divine laws that protect human good. Only the act in accordance with the good can be the path that leads to life.
