contenido: 73. The Christian, thanks to the revelation of God and faith, knows the novelty that marks the morality of his actions; These are called to express the greater or lesser coherence with the dignity and vocation that have been given to them by grace: in Jesus Christ and in his Spirit, the Christian is a new creature, son of God, and through his actions he expresses his conformity or divergence with the image of the Son who is the firstborn among many brothers ([+[0]+]), he lives his fidelity or infidelity to the gift of the Spirit and opens or closes himself to eternal life, to the communion of vision, love and beatitude with God Father, Son and Holy Spirit 123. Christ "forms us according to his image," says Saint Cyril of Alexandria, "so that the features of his divine nature shine in us through sanctification and justice and the good and virtuous life... The beauty of this image shines in us who are in Christ, when, through works, we manifest ourselves as good men" 124.

74. But, on what does the moral qualification of man's free action depend? How is this ordering of human acts towards God ensured? Does it only depend on the intention that is in accordance with the ultimate goal, the supreme good, or on the circumstances - and, in particular, the consequences - that characterize man's actions, or does it not also depend - and above all - on the very object of human acts?

75. But in the context of the effort to develop this rational morality – sometimes called autonomous morality for this reason – there are false solutions, linked particularly to an inadequate understanding of the object of moral action. Some do not sufficiently consider the fact that the will is involved in the concrete choices it makes: these are conditions of its moral goodness and its organization to the ultimate end of the person. Others are also inspired by a conception of freedom that ignores the effective conditions of its exercise, its objective reference to the truth about the good, and its determination through choices of specific behaviors. And thus, according to these theories, free will would be neither morally subject to certain obligations, nor bound by its choices, despite still being responsible for its own acts and their consequences. This “teleologism”, as a method of rediscovering the moral norm, can, then, be called “according to terminologies and approaches taken from different currents of thought” “consequentialism” or “proportionalism”. The first aims to obtain the criteria of the rightness of a given act only from the calculation of the consequences that are expected to arise from the execution of a decision. The second, weighing the values ​​and the goods they pursue against each other, focuses rather on the recognized proportion between the good or bad effects, in view of the greater good or the lesser evil, that are effectively possible in a given situation.

76. These theories can acquire a certain persuasive force due to their affinity with the scientific mentality, concerned, rightly, with ordering technical and economic activities according to the calculation of resources and benefits, procedures and effects. They seek to free one from the impositions of a morality of obligation, voluntaristic and arbitrary, which would be inhuman.

77. To offer the rational criteria for a just moral decision, the aforementioned theories take into account the intention and consequences of human action. Certainly great importance must be given either to the intention – as Jesus insists with particular force in open contrast to the scribes and Pharisees, who meticulously prescribed certain external works without paying attention to the heart ([+[0]+] ) – or to the goods obtained and the evils avoided as a consequence of a particular act. This is a demand for responsibility. But consideration of these consequences – as well as intentions – is not sufficient to assess the moral quality of a specific choice. The weighing of goods and evils, foreseeable as a consequence of an action, is not an adequate method to determine whether the choice of that specific behavior is, according to its kind or in itself, morally good or bad, licit or illicit. Foreseeable consequences belong to those circumstances of the act that, although they can modify the seriousness of a bad action, cannot, however, change the moral species.

78. The morality of the human act depends above all and fundamentally on the object rationally chosen by the deliberate will, as is also proven by the penetrating, still valid, analysis of Saint Thomas 126. Thus, in order to apprehend the object of an act, which specifies it morally, one must place oneself in the perspective of the person who acts. Indeed, the object of the act of willing is a freely chosen behavior. And insofar as it is in accordance with the order of reason, it is the cause of the goodness of the will, it perfects us morally and prepares us to recognize our ultimate goal in the perfect good, original love. Therefore, it cannot be taken as the object of a certain moral act, a process or an event of a physical nature only, which is valued insofar as it originates a certain state of things in the external world. The object is the proximate end of a deliberate choice that determines the act of will of the person who acts. In this sense, as the Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches, "there are concrete behaviors whose choice is always wrong because it entails a disorder of the will, that is, a moral evil." 127. "It frequently happens," Aquinas states, "that man acts with good intentions, but without spiritual benefit because he lacks good will. For example, one steals to help the poor: in this case, although the intention is good, the righteousness of the will is lacking because the works are bad. In conclusion, good intention does not authorize doing any bad deed. "Some say: let us do evil so that good may come. These deserve their own condemnation" ([+[0]+])» 128.

79. Thus, we must reject the thesis, characteristic of teleological and proportionalist theories, according to which it would be impossible to classify as morally bad according to its species – its “object” – the deliberate choice of some specific behaviors or acts regardless of the intention by which the choice is made or of the totality of the foreseeable consequences of that act for all interested persons.

80. Now, reason testifies that there are objects of the human act that are configured as not orderable to God, because they radically contradict the good of the person, created in his image. They are the acts that, in the moral tradition of the Church, have been called intrinsically evil ([+[0]+]): they are always evil for themselves, that is, for their object, regardless of the subsequent intentions of the person acting, and the circumstances. For this reason, without denying in any way the influence that circumstances and, above all, intentions have on morality, the Church teaches that "there are acts that, by themselves and in themselves, regardless of the circumstances, are always seriously illicit by reason of their object" 131. The Second Vatican Council itself, within the framework of the respect due to the human person, offers a broad exemplification of such acts: "Everything that is opposed to life, such as homicides of any kind, genocides, abortion, euthanasia and voluntary suicide itself; everything that violates the integrity of the human person, such as mutilations, physical and mental torture, even attempts at psychological coercion; everything that offends human dignity, such as subhuman living conditions, arbitrary imprisonment, deportations, slavery, prostitution, trafficking of white women and girls; also the ignominious working conditions in which workers are treated as mere instruments of profit, not as free and responsible people; All these things and others like them are certainly disgraces that, by corrupting human civilization, dishonor more to those who practice them than to those who suffer injustice and are totally contrary to the honor due to the Creator" 132.

81. The Church, by teaching the existence of intrinsically evil acts, accepts the doctrine of sacred Scripture. The apostle Paul states categorically: “Do not be deceived! Neither the impure, nor the idolaters, nor the adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor the homosexuals, nor the thieves, nor the covetous, nor the drunkards, nor the abusive, nor the rapacious will inherit the kingdom of God” ([+[0]+]).

82. On the other hand, the intention is good when it aims at the true good of the person in relation to his ultimate goal. But acts, whose object is not ordainable to God and unworthy of the human person, are always and in all cases opposed to this good. In this sense, respect for the rules that prohibit such acts and that require "semper et pro semper", that is, without any exception, not only does not limit good intention, but even constitutes its fundamental expression.

83. As can be seen, in the question of the morality of human acts and particularly in that of the existence of intrinsically evil acts, in a certain sense the very question of man, of his truth and of the moral consequences that derive from it, is concentrated. Recognizing and teaching the existence of intrinsic evil in certain human acts, the Church remains faithful to the integral truth about man and, therefore, respects and promotes him in his dignity and vocation. Consequently, you must reject the theories presented above, which contrast with this truth.

84. The fundamental question that the moral theories recalled above raise with particular intensity is the relationship between the freedom of man and the law of God, that is, the question of the relationship between freedom and truth.

85. The work of discernment of these ethical theories by the Church is not reduced to their denunciation or rejection, but rather seeks to guide with great love all the faithful in the formation of a moral conscience that judges and makes decisions according to truth, as the apostle Paul exhorts: "Do not conform yourselves to the present world, but rather be transformed by the renewal of your mind, so that you can distinguish what the will of God is: what is good, what is pleasing, what is perfect" ( [+[0]+] ). This work of the Church finds its point of support – its formative secret – not so much in doctrinal statements and pastoral exhortations to vigilance, but in having our “gaze” fixed on the Lord Jesus. Every day the Church looks with tireless love at Christ, fully aware that only in him is the true and definitive answer to the moral problem.

86. Rational reflection and daily experience demonstrate the weakness that marks man's freedom. It is real freedom, but contingent. It does not have its absolute and unconditioned origin in itself, but in the existence in which it is found and for which it represents, at the same time, a limit and a possibility. It is the freedom of a creature, that is, a gifted freedom, which must be welcomed like a germ and made to mature responsibly. It is a constitutive part of the creaturely image, which bases the dignity of the person, in which appears the original vocation with which the Creator calls man to the true Good, and even more, through the revelation of Christ, to enter into friendship with him, participating in his same divine life. It is, at the same time, inalienable self-possession and universal openness to each existing being, when it goes out of itself towards knowledge and love for others138. Freedom is based, therefore, on the truth of man and tends towards communion.

87. Christ manifests, above all, that the honest and open recognition of the truth is a condition for authentic freedom: "You will know the truth and the truth will make you free" ( [+[0]+] ) 139. It is the truth that makes one free before power and gives the strength of martyrdom. In this regard, Jesus says before Pilate: "This is why I have come into the world: to bear witness to the truth" ([+[1]+]). Thus true worshipers of God must worship Him “in spirit and in truth” ( [+[2]+] ). By virtue of this worship they become free. Its relationship with the truth and worship of God is manifested in Jesus Christ as the deepest root of freedom.

88. The contrast, indeed, the radical separation between freedom and truth is a consequence, manifestation and realization of another more serious and harmful dichotomy: that between faith and morality.

89. Faith also has a moral content: it inspires and demands a coherent commitment to life; It entails and perfects the reception and observance of divine commandments. As the evangelist John says, “God is Light, in him there is no darkness at all. If we say that we are in communion with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not act the truth... By this we know that we know him: that we keep his commandments. Whoever says: "I know him" and does not keep his commandments is a liar and the truth is not in him. But whoever keeps his word, surely in him the love of God has reached its fullness. By this we know that we are in it. Whoever says that he abides in him, must live as he lived” ( [+[0]+] ).

90. The relationship between faith and morality shines with all its intensity in the unconditional respect that is due to the unavoidable demands of the personal dignity of each man, demands protected by moral norms that prohibit without exception intrinsically evil acts. The universality and immutability of the moral norm manifest and, at the same time, are put at the service of the absolute personal dignity, that is, the inviolability of man, in whose face the splendor of God shines ([+[0]+]).

91. Already in the old alliance we find admirable testimonies of fidelity to the holy law of God carried to the voluntary acceptance of death. Susanna's story is exemplary: to the two unjust judges, who threatened to have her killed if she refused to give in to her impure passion, she responds like this: "What a predicament it constricts me on all sides! If I do this, it is death for me; If I don't, I won't escape from you. But it is better for me to fall into your hands without having done so than to sin before the Lord" ( [+[0]+] ). Susanna, preferring to die innocently in the hands of the judges, testifies not only to her faith and trust in God but also to her obedience to the truth and to the absolute moral order: with her availability to martyrdom, she proclaims that it is not fair to do what God's law classifies as evil in order to derive some good from it. Susana chooses for herself the best part: a very clear testimony, without any compromise, of the truth and the God of Israel, over the good; In this way, he manifests the holiness of God in his actions.

92. In martyrdom, as confirmation of the inviolability of the moral order, the sanctity of God's law and at the same time the intangibility of the personal dignity of man, created in the image and likeness of God, shine. It is a dignity that can never be debased or contrasted, even with good intentions, whatever the difficulties. Jesus exhorts us with the utmost severity: "What does it profit a man to gain the whole world if he ruins his life?" ( [+[0]+] ).

93. Finally, martyrdom is a clear sign of the sanctity of the Church: fidelity to God's holy law, witnessed by death, is a solemn announcement and missionary commitment "usque ad sanguinem" so that the splendor of moral truth is not obscured in the customs and mentality of people and society. Such testimony has an extraordinary value so that not only in civil society but even within the ecclesial communities themselves we do not fall into the most dangerous crisis that can affect man: the confusion of good and evil, which makes it impossible to build and preserve the moral order of individuals and communities. The martyrs, and more broadly all the saints in the Church, with the eloquent and fascinating example of a life totally transfigured by the splendor of moral truth, illuminate each era of history, awakening the moral sense. Bearing witness to the good, they represent a living reproach to those who transgress the law ( [+[0]+] ) and make the words of the prophet resonate with permanent relevance: «Alas, those who call evil good, and good evil; who give darkness for light, and light for darkness; who give bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter! ( [+[1]+] ).

94. In bearing witness to absolute moral good, Christians are not alone. They find confirmation in the moral sense of the people and in the great religious and wisdom traditions of the West and the East, which highlight the interior and mysterious action of the Spirit of God. The expression of the Latin poet Juvenal is valid for everyone: "Consider it the greatest crime to prefer survival to modesty and, for the love of life, to lose the meaning of living." 147. The voice of conscience has always remembered without ambiguity that there are truths and moral values ​​for which one must be willing to even give one's life. In the word and above all in the sacrifice of life for moral value, the Church gives the same testimony of that truth that, already present in creation, shines fully in the face of Christ: "We know," says Saint Justin, "that those who have followed the doctrines of the Stoics have also been hated and killed, due to the fact that they have demonstrated wisdom at least in the formulation of moral doctrine, thanks to the seed of the Word that is in every human race." 148.

95. The doctrine of the Church, and in particular its firmness in defending the universal and permanent validity of the precepts that prohibit intrinsically evil acts, is not infrequently judged as a sign of intolerable intransigence, especially in the enormously complex and conflictive situations of the moral life of man and of today's society. Such intransigence would be in contrast to the maternal condition of the Church. This one, it is said, does not show understanding and compassion. But, in reality, the motherhood of the Church can never be separated from her teaching mission, which she must always carry out as the faithful wife of Christ, who is the truth in person: "As a Teacher, she never tires of proclaiming the moral norm... Of such a norm the Church is certainly neither the author nor the arbiter. In obedience to the truth that is Christ, whose image is reflected in the nature and dignity of the human person, the Church interprets the moral norm and proposes it to all men of good will, without hiding the demands of radicality and perfection" 149.

96. The firmness of the Church in defending universal and immutable moral norms has nothing humiliating. It is only at the service of man's true freedom. Since there is no freedom outside or against the truth, the categorical defense – that is, without concessions or compromises – of the absolutely inalienable demands of man's personal dignity must be considered the path and condition for the very existence of freedom.

97. In this way, moral norms, and first of all the negative ones, which prohibit evil, manifest their meaning and their personal and social force. By protecting the inviolable personal dignity of each man, they help the very conservation of the human social fabric and its straight and fruitful development. In particular, the commandments of the second table of the Decalogue, also remembered by Jesus to the young man in the gospel ([+[0]+]), constitute the primordial rules of all social life.

98. Faced with the serious forms of social and economic injustice, as well as political corruption suffered by entire peoples and nations, the indignant reaction of many people who are oppressed and humiliated in their fundamental human rights is increasing, and the need for a radical personal and social renewal capable of ensuring justice, solidarity, honesty and transparency is becoming increasingly widespread and intensified.

99. Only God, the supreme Good, is the immovable basis and the irreplaceable condition of morality, and therefore of the commandments, particularly the negative ones, which always and in all cases prohibit behavior and acts incompatible with the personal dignity of each man. Thus, the supreme Good and the moral good are found in truth: the truth of God the Creator and Redeemer, and the truth of man created and redeemed by him. Only on this truth is it possible to build a renewed society and resolve the complex and serious problems that affect it, above all that of overcoming the most diverse forms of totalitarianism to open the way to authentic freedom of the person. «Totalitarianism is born from the denial of the truth in an objective sense. If there is no transcendent truth, with whose obedience man conquers his full identity, there is no secure principle that guarantees just relations between men: the interests of class, group or nation inevitably oppose them to each other. If the transcendent truth is not recognized, the force of power triumphs, and each person tends to use to the extreme the means at his disposal to impose his own interest or his own opinion, without respecting the rights of others... The root of modern totalitarianism must be seen, therefore, in the denial of the transcendent dignity of the human person, the visible image of the invisible God and, precisely for this reason, the natural subject of rights that no one can violate: neither the individual, nor the group, nor the social class, nor the nation, nor the State. Nor can the majority of a social body do so, standing against the minority, marginalizing it, oppressing it, exploiting it or even trying to destroy it" 155.

100. In this regard, the Catechism of the Catholic Church, after stating: “in economic matters, respect for human dignity requires the practice of the virtue of temperance, to moderate attachment to the goods of this world; of the virtue of justice, to preserve the rights of others and give them what is due to them; and solidarity, following the golden rule and according to the generosity of the Lord, who "though he was rich, for your sakes he became poor so that you might become rich through his poverty" ( [+[0]+] )» 157, presents a series of behaviors and acts that are in contrast with human dignity: theft, deliberately retaining things received as a loan or lost items, commercial fraud ( [+[1]+] ), unjust wages ( [+[2]+] ), raising prices by speculating on the ignorance and needs of others ([+[3]+]), the appropriation and private use of a company's social assets, poorly performed work, tax fraud, falsification of checks and invoices, excessive expenses, waste, etc. 158. And it must be added: «The seventh commandment proscribes acts or companies that, for one reason or another, selfish or ideological, commercial or totalitarian, lead to enslaving human beings, to despising their personal dignity, to buying them, selling them and exchanging them as merchandise. It is a sin against the dignity of people and their fundamental rights to reduce them through violence to the status of an object of consumption or a source of profit. Saint Paul commanded a Christian master to treat his Christian slave "not as a slave, but... as a brother... in the Lord" ([+[4]+] )" 159.

101. In the political sphere, it must be noted that truthfulness in the relationships between rulers and governed; transparency in public administration; impartiality in the service of public affairs; respect for the rights of political opponents; the protection of the rights of the accused against summary trials and convictions; the fair and honest use of public money; The rejection of equivocal or illicit means to conquer, maintain or increase power at any cost, are principles that have their fundamental basis - as well as their singular urgency - in the transcendent value of the person and in the objective moral demands of the functioning of the States 160. When these principles are not observed, the very foundation of political coexistence suffers and all social life is progressively compromised, threatened and doomed to its dissolution ( [+[0]+] ). After the fall, in many countries, of the ideologies that conditioned politics to a totalitarian conception of the world - the first among them being Marxism - there exists today a no less serious risk due to the denial of the fundamental rights of the human person and the absorption in politics of the same religious concern that lives in the heart of every human being: it is the risk of the alliance between democracy and ethical relativism, which removes from civil coexistence any safe point of reference. morality, stripping it more radically of the recognition of truth. In effect, "if there is no ultimate truth âthat guides and orients political actionâ then human ideas and convictions can easily be exploited for purposes of power. A democracy without values ​​easily turns into visible or covert totalitarianism, as history shows” 161.

102. Even in the most difficult situations, man must observe the moral standard to be obedient to the sacred commandment of God and consistent with his own personal dignity. Certainly, the harmony between freedom and truth sometimes requires unusual sacrifices and is achieved at a high price: it can even entail martyrdom. But, as universal and everyday experience demonstrates, man is tempted to break this harmony: "I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate... I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want" ([+[0]+]).
103. The spiritual realm of hope is always open to man, with the help of divine grace and with the collaboration of human freedom.

104. In this context, the right space is opened for God's mercy for the sinner who converts, and for understanding human weakness. This understanding never means compromising and falsifying the measure of good and evil to adapt it to circumstances. While it is human that man, having sinned, recognizes his weakness and asks for mercy for his own faults, on the other hand, the attitude of those who make their own weakness the criterion of truth about good is unacceptable, so that they can feel justified by themselves, even without needing to resort to God and his mercy. Such an attitude corrupts the morality of the entire society, because it teaches us to doubt the objectivity of the moral law in general and to reject absolute moral prohibitions on certain human acts, and ends up confusing all value judgments.

105. Great vigilance is asked of everyone to avoid being infected by the pharisaical attitude, which seeks to eliminate the awareness of one's own limit and one's own sin, and which today manifests itself particularly with the attempt to adapt the moral norm to one's own abilities and one's own interests, and even with the rejection of the very concept of norm. On the contrary, accepting the disproportion between law and human capacity, that is, the capacity of the moral forces alone of man left to himself, arouses the desire for grace and predisposes one to receive it. "Who will free me from this body that leads me to death?" Saint Paul asks. And with joyful and grateful confession he responds: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” ( [+[0]+] ).

106. Evangelization is the most peremptory and demanding challenge that the Church has been called to face from its very origins. In reality, this challenge is not only posed by the social and cultural situations that the Church encounters throughout history, but is contained in the mandate of the resurrected Jesus, which defines the very reason for the Church's existence: "Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to all creation" ( [+[0]+] ).

107. Evangelization – and therefore the “new evangelization” – also involves the proclamation and the moral proposal. Jesus himself, by preaching precisely the kingdom of God and his saving love, has made a call to faith and conversion ( [+[0]+] ). And Peter with the other Apostles, announcing the resurrection of Jesus of Nazareth from the dead, proposes a new life that must be lived, a path that must be followed to be a disciple of the Risen One ( [+[1]+] ).

108. At the root of the new evangelization and the new moral life, which it proposes and raises in its fruits of holiness and missionary action, is the Spirit of Christ, the principle and strength of the fruitfulness of Holy Mother Church, as Paul VI reminds us: "There will never be evangelization possible without the action of the Holy Spirit"167. To the Spirit of Jesus, welcomed by the humble and docile heart of the believer, is due, therefore, the flourishing of Christian moral life and the witness of holiness in the great variety of vocations, gifts, responsibilities and conditions and situations of life. It is the Holy Spirit - Novatian already affirmed, expressing in this way the authentic faith of the Church - "the one who has given firmness to the souls and minds of the disciples, the one who has illuminated divine things in them; Strengthened by him, the disciples were not afraid of prisons or chains for the name of the Lord; Furthermore, they despised the very powers and torments of the world, now armed and strengthened through it, having within themselves the gifts that this same Spirit donates and sends like jewels to the Church, bride of Christ. Indeed, it is he who raises up the prophets in the Church, instructs the teachers, suggests the words, performs wonders and healings, produces admirable works, grants the discernment of spirits, assigns the tasks of government, inspires counsel, distributes and harmonizes any other charismatic gift and, by this, completely perfects, everywhere and in everything, the Church of the Lord" 168.

109. The entire Church, a participant in the "munus propheticum" of the Lord Jesus through the gift of his Spirit, is called to evangelization and witness to a life of faith. Thanks to the permanent presence in it of the Spirit of truth ([+[0]+]), "the totality of the faithful, who have the anointing of the Holy One ([+[1]+]) cannot be mistaken when they believe, and this peculiar prerogative of theirs is manifested through the supernatural sense of faith of the entire people when "from the bishops to the last lay faithful" gives their universal consent in matters of faith and customs" 169.

110. What has been said so far about theology in general, can and should be proposed anew for moral theology, understood in its specificity of scientific reflection on the Gospel as a gift and commandment of new life, on life according to "the truth in love" ([+[0]+]), on the life of holiness of the Church, that is, on the life in which the truth of good shines, carried to its perfection. Not only in the area of faith, but also and inseparably in the area of morality, the Magisterium of the Church intervenes, whose task is to "discern, through normative judgments for the conscience of the faithful, the acts that in themselves are in accordance with the demands of faith and promote its expression in life, as well as those that, on the contrary, due to their malice are incompatible with these demands" 172. Preaching the commandments of God and the charity of Christ, the Magisterium of the Church also teaches the faithful the particular and determined precepts, and asks them to consider them as morally obligatory in conscience. Furthermore, it carries out an important task of vigilance, warning the faithful of the presence of possible errors, even just implicit ones, when their conscience fails to recognize the accuracy and truth of the moral rules taught by the Magisterium.

111. The service that moralistic theologians are called to offer at the present time is of primary importance, not only for the life and mission of the Church, but also for society and human culture. It is their responsibility, in intimate and vital connection with biblical and dogmatic theology, to underline in scientific reflection "the dynamic aspect that helps to highlight the response that man must give to the divine call in the process of his growth in love, within a saving community. In this way, moral theology will reach an internal spiritual dimension, responding to the demands of full development of the "imago Dei" that is in man, and to the laws of the spiritual process described in Christian asceticism and mysticism» 176.

112. The moral theologian must apply, therefore, the necessary discernment in the context of current culture, predominantly scientific and technical, exposed to the danger of pragmatism and positivism. From the theological point of view, moral principles are not dependent on the historical moment in which they come to light. The fact that some believers act without observing the teachings of the Magisterium or, erroneously, consider their conduct as morally just when it is contrary to the law of God declared by their pastors, cannot constitute a valid argument to reject the truth of the moral norms taught by the Church. The affirmation of moral principles is not the responsibility of empirical-formal methods. Moral theology, faithful to the supernatural sense of faith, without rejecting the validity of such methods, but without limiting its perspective to them, looks above all at the spiritual dimension of the human heart and its vocation to divine love.

113. The teaching of moral doctrine implies the conscious assumption of these intellectual, spiritual and pastoral responsibilities. For this reason, moral theologians, who accept the function of teaching the doctrine of the Church, have the grave duty of educating the faithful in this moral discernment, in the commitment to true good and in confidently resorting to divine grace.

114. The responsibility of faith and the life of faith of the people of God weighs in a peculiar and proper way on pastors, as the Second Vatican Council reminds us: «Among the main functions of bishops, the proclamation of the Gospel stands out. Indeed, bishops are the preachers of the Gospel who bring new disciples to Christ. They are also the authentic teachers, because they are endowed with the authority of Christ. They preach to the people that they have entrusted the faith that must be believed and that must be put into practice and they illuminate it with the light of the Holy Spirit. Drawing from the treasure of Revelation the new and the old ([+[0]+]), they make it bear fruit and with their vigilance they remove the errors that threaten their flock ([+[1]+])» 178.

115. In fact, it is the first time that the Magisterium of the Church exposes with some breadth the fundamental elements of this doctrine, presenting the reasons for the pastoral discernment necessary in complex and even critical practical and cultural situations.

116. As bishops, we have the duty to ensure that the word of God is taught faithfully. It is part of our pastoral ministry, beloved brothers in the episcopate, to monitor the faithful transmission of this moral teaching and to resort to appropriate measures so that the faithful are preserved from any doctrine and theory contrary to it. Theologians help us all in this task; However, theological opinions do not constitute the rule or norm of our teaching. Its authority derives, with the assistance of the Holy Spirit and in communion "cum Petro et sub Petro", from our fidelity to the Catholic faith received from the Apostles. As bishops we have the serious obligation to personally ensure that the "sound doctrine" ( [+[0]+] ) of faith and morals is taught in our dioceses.

117. In the heart of the Christian, in the most secret core of man, the question that the young man in the Gospel addressed one day to Jesus always resonates: "Teacher, what good must I do to obtain eternal life?" ( [+[0]+] ). But it is necessary that each one direct it to the "good" Master, because he is the only one who can respond in the fullness of the truth, in any situation, in the most diverse circumstances. And when Christians ask him the question that arises from their consciences, the Lord responds with the words of the new alliance entrusted to his Church. Now, as the Apostle says of himself, we are sent “to preach the Gospel. And not with wise words, so as not to distort the cross of Christ" ( [+[1]+] ). For this reason, the Church's answer to man's question has the wisdom and strength of Christ crucified, the Truth that is donated.

118. In concluding these considerations, we entrust to Mary, Mother of God and Mother of Mercy, our persons, the sufferings and joys of our existence, the moral life of believers and men of good will, the research of moral scholars.

119. This is the consoling certainty of the Christian faith, to which it owes its profound humanity and extraordinary simplicity. Sometimes, in discussions of new and complex moral problems, it may seem as if Christian morality were itself too difficult: arduous to understand and almost impossible to practice. This is false, because "in terms of evangelical simplicity" it fundamentally consists of following Jesus Christ, abandoning oneself to him, allowing oneself to be transformed by his grace and to be renewed by his mercy, which are achieved in the life of communion of his Church. «Whoever wants to live, Saint Augustine reminds us, has somewhere to live, has somewhere to live from. Let him come closer, let him believe, let him be incorporated to be vivified. "Do not avoid the company of the members" 182. With the light of the Spirit, anyone can understand it, even the least learned, especially those who know how to keep a "whole heart" ( [+[0]+] ). On the other hand, this evangelical simplicity does not exempt us from facing the complexity of reality, but it can lead to its truest understanding because following Christ will progressively clarify the characteristics of authentic Christian morality and, at the same time, will provide the vital force for its realization. Ensuring that the dynamism of following Christ develops organically, without its moral demands being falsified or ignored - with all the consequences that this entails - is the task of the Magisterium of the Church. Whoever loves Christ observes his commandments ( [+[1]+] ).

120. Mary is also Mother of mercy because Jesus entrusts his Church and all humanity to her. At the foot of the cross, when he accepts Juan as his son; When, together with Christ, she asks the Father for forgiveness for those who do not know what they are doing ( [+[0]+] ), Mary, with perfect docility to the Spirit, experiences the richness and universality of God's love, which expands her heart and enables her to embrace the entire human race. In this way, she gives herself to us as the Mother of each and every one of us. She becomes the Mother who reaches us with divine mercy.
